title: Welcoming birth
hook: the other end of life: traditions welcome birth

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Prophet's first words on waking. Your line was awake again. Were your first words this morning thanks? Today, a different kind of waking: a life arriving. Day eight hundred sixteen.

A hospital corridor at three in the morning, or a bedroom at home, or a car that didn't make it in time. A small, furious, astonished person has just arrived, and the room changes. This stretch of the path has been about the end of life: rites for the dying, words for the grieving, letters for after. It would be lopsided to leave out the other end. The traditions that mourn the dead also have ways of greeting the newborn. Today: three welcomes, from three homes, each in its own words.
screen: `A SMALL PERSON ARRIVES.` → `THE OTHER END OF LIFE.` → `THREE WELCOMES.`

segments.voice: First, a waiting man holds a baby. In Luke's Gospel, Mary and Joseph bring the infant Jesus to the Temple, and a man named Simeon, who has been told he won't see death before he sees the Lord's Christ, takes him: "Then took he him up in his arms, and blessed God." His song follows, and it begins with his own death: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace." At the very start of one life, another man says he's ready to go. Birth and death, in one pair of arms. Second, a call whispered in the ear. In Muslim tradition, the call to prayer, the adhan, may be softly spoken into a newborn's right ear, so that among the first words the child hears are the words that call people to prayer. Some hadith collections report the Prophet ﷺ doing this for his grandson. Third, a name from an open page. In a Sikh naming ceremony, the family gathers before the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture is opened, and a passage is read. The first letter of that passage guides the first letter of the child's name. The scripture, in a sense, joins in the naming. Fourth, welcome in other homes. Elsewhere, Christian families may baptize or dedicate a child, Jewish families may hold a naming or a brit, Hindu families have their own rites for name and first food, and Buddhist families may bring a baby for blessing. Each has its own meaning, kept in its own home. What they share is simple: a new person is not just born, but received.
screen: `SIMEON HOLDS A BABY.` · `A CALL WHISPERED IN THE EAR.` · `A NAME FROM AN OPEN PAGE.` · `WELCOME IN OTHER HOMES.` · then, large: `WELCOMING BIRTH.`

segments.voice: Think of someone new in your life, or about to be: a baby in the family or among friends, a new neighbor, a new colleague, a child just starting school. Hold them in mind for a few breaths. Let a sense of welcome gather, the way it might if you were holding them. If you pray, you can bless them in the words of your own tradition. Then decide one small act of welcome for today: a note, a meal, a greeting, a name remembered. Rest. The bell holds the time.
Welcoming birth. How traditions receive a new life: Simeon's arms, the adhan in a newborn's ear, a Sikh name from an open page. Today's word.
Your line: welcome. Today, do one small act of welcome for someone new, and say their name when you do it. Day eight hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Muslim families may whisper the adhan in a newborn's right ear; Sikh families name a child from a passage of the Guru Granth Sahib; Christian families may baptize or dedicate children, and Jewish families may hold a naming or a brit.

notes: Editor pass: Luke doesn't call Simeon old or say how long he waited, so 'old man' and 'waiting a long time' were replaced with what Luke 2:26 says; cut the superlative 'biggest waking of all', 'weeks of this path' and 'often' (adhan); 'bury the dead' became 'mourn the dead' since some of these traditions cremate.
The index hook says 'every tradition welcomes birth'; the script avoids 'every' under the claims rule and speaks of 'the traditions' and named examples.
Check hadith numbers for the Prophet giving the adhan in al-Hasan's ear (Abu Dawud 5105, Tirmidhi 1514); an Islam Keeper should confirm and may note that scholars grade this report differently.
Sikh naming: the first letter of the hukam guiding the name's first letter is standard practice (described in the Sikh Rehat Maryada); a Sikh Keeper should confirm.
Simeon is described only by what Luke 2:25–27 says (waiting for the consolation of Israel, told he would see the Lord's Christ, came by the Spirit into the Temple); no age is given.
'Hindus have their own rites for name and first food' (namakarana, annaprashana) and 'Buddhists may bring a baby for blessing' are brief; the relevant Keepers should confirm.
The hook's 'three in the morning' is a scene detail, not a claim.

Audit 2026-10-01: the fork's wrong option 'you bless the parents' was not wrong, since Simeon does bless them (Luke 2:34); replaced it, removed the unsourced 'young couple' and 'waiting in the Temple' (Luke 2:27 says he came in by the Spirit), and renamed the unclear fourth head 'welcome, at both ends'. Note for an Islam Keeper: the Abu Dawud/Tirmidhi report does not itself say 'right ear'; that detail is custom.
